from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        lecture_lines = ["Data has a shape called a distribution.", "Every outcome is equally likely here.", "Many rolls form a uniform rectangle."]

        self.place_at_grid(text_label, 'B2')
        self.play(Write(text_label))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Show a histogram of a Normal distribution (#00FF00) fading in.
        # Constructing a simple bar chart to represent a distribution shape
        hist = VGroup(*[Rectangle(height=0.5 + i*0.2, width=0.4, color="#00FF00", fill_opacity=0.8) for i in range(5)]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        self.place_at_grid(hist, 'D3')
        self.play(FadeIn(hist))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#00FF00")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===

        peak = hist[2]
        highlight = SurroundingRectangle(peak, color="#FF0000", buff=0.05)
        self.play(Create(highlight))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FF0000")
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Problem: The Chaos of Small Samples", [
            "Real-world data is rarely normal.", 
            "Most distributions are skewed or erratic.", 
            "Small samples lead to inconsistent predictions."

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["The CLT reveals a hidden pattern.", "Sample means always approach a Bell Curve.", "This holds regardless of population shape.", "More samples make the curve clearer.", "Averages magically form a symmetrical distribution."]
        self.setup_layout("The CLT Core Mechanism: The Power of Averages", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # "Display text: 'Averaging samples stabilizes erratic data.' in #FFFFFF."
        text = Text("Averaging samples stabilizes erratic data.", font_size=32, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(text, 'B2')
        self.play(Write(text))
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(1)
        self.play(FadeOut(text))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # "Show multiple small sample means animating towards the center (#FFFF00)."
        dots = VGroup(*[Dot(color=YELLOW) for _ in range(20)])
        for dot in dots:
            start_pos = np.array([np.random.uniform(2, 6), np.random.uniform(-2, 2), 0])
            dot.move_to(start_pos)
        self.add(dots)
        self.play(
            *[dot.animate.move_to(self.grid['C4']) for dot in dots],
            run_time=2
        )
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # "Transition into a single larger Normal distribution shape (#00FF00)."
        bell_curve = FunctionGraph(
            lambda x: np.exp(-(x**2)/2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi),
            x_range=[-3, 3],
            color=GREEN
        )
        self.place_in_area(bell_curve, 'C2', 'E5')
        self.play(Create(bell_curve))
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["The magic number is thirty.", "Sample size affects the curve's shape.", "Larger samples reduce standard error.", "The Bell Curve becomes more precise.", "Precision increases with more data points."]
        self.setup_layout("The 'Sample Size' Rule", lecture_lines)
        
        # Mobjects
        text_label = Text("Bigger samples reveal the true shape.", font_size=24, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(text_label, 'A1')
        
        # N=5 Curve
        def get_normal_curve(sigma):
            return FunctionGraph(
                lambda x: (1 / (sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))) * np.exp(-0.5 * (x / sigma) ** 2),
                x_range=[-3, 3], color=WHITE
            )
            
        curve_n5 = get_normal_curve(sigma=1.2)
        curve_n30 = get_normal_curve(sigma=0.5)
        
        # Area for curves
        self.place_in_area(curve_n5, 'C2', 'E5', scale_factor=0.8)
        self.place_in_area(curve_n30, 'C2', 'E5', scale_factor=0.8)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FF00FF"), Write(text_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FF00FF"), Create(curve_n5))
        curve_n5.set_color("#FF00FF")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#00FF00"))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color("#00FF00"), Transform(curve_n5, curve_n30))
        curve_n5.set_color("#00FF00")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color("#00FF00"))
        self.wait(1)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "The CLT allows reliable population inferences.",
            "We use small samples to estimate reality.",
            "It guarantees accuracy in mass quality control.",
            "Confidence intervals predict large-scale outcomes.",
            "Statistics makes massive data manageable."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Real-World Application", lecture_lines)
        
        # Elements

        sample_bar = Rectangle(height=0.5, width=2.0, fill_color=YELLOW, fill_opacity=0.8, stroke_width=0)

outline.topic: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): The Magic of Bell Curves

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Distributions
sections.content: Briefly define a 'distribution' as the shape data takes. Introduce the 'Uniform Distribution' (where every outcome is equally likely, like rolling a fair die) as our starting point.
sections.example: A visual animation showing a die roll. After 6 rolls, the bar chart is jagged; after 600 rolls, the bars are almost perfectly flat—a rectangle.

sections.title: The Problem: The Chaos of Small Samples
sections.content: Explain that real-world data is rarely 'normal' or pretty. Most things are skewed, erratic, or flat. Introduce the challenge: How do we make predictions if the population distribution is weird?
sections.example: Visualize a 'Claw' distribution (highly irregular). Show a character, 'Robo-Dog', trying to predict the average height of its puppies based on only two random samples—the results are wildly inconsistent.

sections.title: The CLT Core Mechanism: The Power of Averages
sections.content: Introduce the CLT: Regardless of the population's shape, the distribution of the *sample means* will always approach a Normal Distribution (Bell Curve) as the sample size increases.
sections.example: Animation: Take 5 samples from the 'Claw' distribution, calculate the mean, and plot it. Repeat 1,000 times. As the animation speeds up, the messy dots magically stack into a perfect symmetrical Bell Curve.

sections.title: The 'Sample Size' Rule
sections.content: Emphasize the 'magic number' (n ≥ 30). Explain that as the sample size grows, the standard error decreases, making the Bell Curve narrower and more precise.
sections.example: Compare two graphs: Sample size 5 (a wide, bumpy bell) vs. Sample size 50 (a tall, sharp, centered bell). Use a 'Precision Gauge' icon that fills up as sample size increases.

sections.title: Real-World Application
sections.content: Summarize the significance: The CLT allows us to use Z-scores and confidence intervals to make inferences about massive populations using only small, manageable samples.
sections.example: Scenario: A quality control robot checking the weight of millions of jellybeans. Instead of weighing every single one, it takes small groups of 30, calculates the mean, and uses the CLT to guarantee the batch quality with 95% confidence.
